title: Numbers in letters
hookLine: each letter has a number value; chai is eighteen

cards: That's the number Genesis gives when Abram hears his nephew Lot has been carried off by raiding kings: "he armed his trained servants, born in his own house, three hundred and eighteen," and went after them.
An oddly exact number for a rescue party. A reader could pass right over it. One rabbi in the Talmud didn't.
He looked at three hundred and eighteen and saw a person. To see what he saw, you need one fact: Hebrew letters can also be read as numbers.

teach.b: Gematria. In Hebrew, each letter carries a number. Alef is one, bet is two, and so on up to yod, ten; then the tens, then the hundreds.
So any word has a sum. First, one you may have seen on a necklace.
Chai, alive, is two letters: chet, eight, and yod, ten. Together, eighteen.
That's why eighteen carries a quiet meaning in Jewish life; some families give gifts in multiples of eighteen, wishing someone life along with the money. Second, back to Abram.
The Talmud records a teacher who said those three hundred and eighteen men were really one man: Eliezer, Abram's servant. Add the letters of Eliezer, and they come to three hundred and eighteen.
Read that way, Abram went to the rescue with one faithful helper, and the number was a name in disguise. Third, a sense of proportion. Pirkei Avot gives gematria its place.

Rabbi Eliezer ben Chisma calls certain detailed laws the essentials, and calls gematria, along with the study of the heavens, the after-courses of wisdom. The side dishes: delicious, worth having, but not the meal.
Even inside the tradition, the game has its place at the table. Fourth, an ordinary day. Gematria trains a reader to notice.
A number that looks like filler might be worth a second look; a word might hold more than its first meaning. The letters aren't only sounds.

how: Hebrew letters double as numbers, and gematria finds meaning in the sums; some Jewish families give gifts in multiples of eighteen, the value of chai, and Pirkei Avot calls gematria one of the after-courses of wisdom.

games.q: you're reading Genesis: Abram goes to rescue Lot with three hundred and eighteen men. one rabbi in the Talmud stops at the number. what does he see?
o: a count of the tribes and their households.
the name of Abram's servant, Eliezer, hidden in the sum.
games.why: the letters of Eliezer add up to 318, so he reads it as Abram going with one faithful helper. a number becomes a name.

practice: If you know how your name, or a Hebrew name you love, is written in Hebrew letters, add up the values slowly, one letter at a time; if not, start with chai: chet is eight, yod is ten.
Then let the sum go and sit with the word itself, and what it holds for you: a person, a memory, a hope. If you pray, you can give thanks for the life the word chai names.

wordCard.voice: Gematria. Reading Hebrew letters as numbers, and finding meaning in the sums. Chai is eighteen; Abram's three hundred and eighteen, one reading says, is Eliezer. Today's word.
